Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Last Thursday, the Washington Post website carried an AP story that was largely ignored elsewhere, “Marijuana Big Earner for Mexico Gangs. ” However, the Post printed only a brief excerpt in the paper. 

It was both prohibitionist propaganda – demonstrating once again that the Drug War is really about marijuana – and an indication that the situation in Mexico may be about to get much worse. And US prisons are going to be even more overcrowded, and the borders will become even more violent.

 

It seems that Drug Czar John Walters and U.S. federal prosecutors from the border region were at a conference at a resort in Los Cabos, in Baja California, meeting with Mexican Attorney General Eduardo Medina Mora. 

Incredibly, the Mexican AG seems to have been urging the US to federally prosecute more impoverished Mexicans who are carrying relatively small amounts of marijuana across the border, which is somehow supposed to hurt the “cartels.” The puppet is asking the puppeteer to arrest his own people. The Canadian police have done essentially the same thing. 

See 

Marc Emery Forced to Accept Plea Bargain for Five Years in A Canadian Prison. Charges Against Co-Defendants to Be Dropped. Canada Betrays Its Citizens and Its Sovereignty. 

and 

RCMP = Really Conservative Marijuana Police: Law Enforcement, Prohibition and Democracy. Are More Americans In Favor Legalization than Canadians? Politicians Ignore the People, Who Ignore Police. 

The AP says, “Mexican officials have complained that U.S. prosecutors often release small or mid-level traffickers caught with a few dozen pounds of marijuana.” 

Of course, Walters agreed. He called the AP reporter in Mexico City to tell him, "We're trying to increase the force with which we're attacking this problem. This is a focus because of the overlooked importance marijuana has in the violence." 

See 

New York Times Cheers "MEXICO TO JOIN US IN FIGHT ON DRUGS – Treaty is expected to cut down smuggling across border and break up gangs of dealers." We Couldn’t Make This Up! 

Naturally, the federal prosecutors are in favor of having their budgets increased, but there will also have to be increases in the budgets for jails and prisons. After all, there was a reason that most of the small-time smugglers have not been prosecuted, and it was not because the US Attorneys are really closet NORML members.

Walters claimed that marijuana earns the Mexican gangs, wrongly called “cartels”, an estimated “$8.5 billion or about 61 percent of their annual estimated income of $13.8 billion. Cocaine sales earn the cartels about $3.9 billion, and methamphetamine about $1 billion.”
See 

Now, How the Narks Created Smack in Mexico. Replacing Marijuana With Poppies. The Iron Law of Prohibition Keeps Working, But The Media Don’t 

In reality, no one really knows how much marijuana – or heroin, or cocaine, or meth, comes across the border every year. These numbers are mostly BS. It is the nature of contraband markets that no one really knows their size. 

See 

Where Have All the BC Buds Gone? Tighter Borders and Falling Greenback Reveal Illusion of Prohibition Fostered by Both Sides. BS After All? 

On January 2, 2007, The Arizona Republic reported that the Border Patrol in Arizona alone “seized over 331 tons (662,650 pounds) of marijuana worth $530 million last fiscal year, ending September 30, 2006. That set a record for the fifth straight year. It nearly equaled the 350 tons seized in California, Texas and New Mexico combined…. On December 6, 2006 agents seized an estimated $4.2 million worth of pot crammed inside two pickups in Nogales.” 

Seizure volumes – not prices – are the only hard numbers in the equation, but it should be clear that prosecuting people with “a few dozen pounds of marijuana” is not going to have any impact on the total dollar volume. In fact, it might actually increase it by reducing the supply, and thus help the big “organized crime” gangs by eliminating their smaller  competitors. 

It may also increase the violence along the border as small smugglers resist arrest. The AP article ended by saying, “Since taking office in December 2006, Mexican President Felipe Calderon has sent thousands of soldiers and police to violence-plagued states to combat drug gangs.” 

See 

Will “Plan Mexico” And Its Surge in the Drug War Put Prohibition On the Public Agenda? Analysis by Richard Cowan 

and 

Lou Dobbs and the Second Mexican War. Has It Already Begun? Counting the Costs of the Drugwar. 

What Mexico really needs is for the US to legalize marijuana and end the black market on both sides of the border. Bringing the Mexican military into the Drug War has been a disaster, and it is certain to get worse. 

Today, the Future of Freedom Foundation website printed an excellent article, Common Sense and the Drug Problem, by a Laredo businessman, Hank Sames, who noted, “All of these factors create a climate of fear in Mexico and a reduction in opportunity for those who want a legitimate job. The rich either leave the country or build fortresses to live in and surround themselves with bodyguards. The poor oftentimes become part of the criminal element because of the money to be made in the illegal-drug trade. For every drug criminal Mexico captures or kills, there is a new one eager and ready to replace him. 

Mexico is in danger of collapsing under this cancer.” 

Although the Post generally follows the prohibitionist party line rather slavishly, on February 14th, it published a lengthy article, “Mexican Rights Panel Called 'Disappointing' Report Cites Lack of Focus on Military ”, By Manuel Roig-Franzia. I recommend that you read the complete article. (Registration is required, but it is free.) 

It reported, “A leading U.S. human rights group said Wednesday that Mexico's national human rights commission fails to press the military to end abusive practices and ‘has helped create an atmosphere of distrust.’ 

In a 128-page report released in Mexico City, the New York-based advocacy group Human Rights Watch concluded that Mexico's commission "is failing to live up to its promise" and is "tolerating abusive practices." The report said the commission "has been disappointing," despite having a $73 million annual budget and 1,000 employees, making it "by far the largest of any ombudsman's office in the Americas and one of the largest in the world." 

In a statement late Wednesday, the commission said that "many of the assertions in this report are unsupportable because they propose actions and conduct that exceed the legal limit of this institution." 

The report adds to a crescendo of recent complaints about human rights abuses in Mexico. In the past week, Amnesty International and the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights have raised concerns about abuses allegedly committed by the military during President Felipe Calderon's 14-month campaign against drug cartels. Numerous rights groups have called for the military to end its role in that effort.” 

See also, 

Mexico, the Drugwar and the US National Interest: Never Mind Iraq; We Need To Pay Attention to What We Are Doing to Our Southern Neighbor. 

Ironically, on the same day, the leftist Counterpunch also published a long piece , Flying Heads at Mexico City Airport Drug War Mayhem Boils Over From Border to Border , by John Ross, which gave the grisly details about the violence of the war in Mexico. 

“Calderon's military offensive has failed to stem the harvest of death. Last year, with the troops in the field, 2791 victims (7.3 a day) were registered by authorities, 500 more than the 2221 counted in 2006 when the army was still under wraps. During the first 15 days of 2008, 114 victims were recorded - 11.7 a day - compared with 174 for the entire month of January 2007 - perhaps a fifth of the dead were beheaded or otherwise mutilated.” 

But all of this will be solved, if the US would just prosecute more peasants “with a few dozen pounds of marijuana.” 

See 

Bush Should Have John – Comical Ali – Walters Explain The Iraq War, Then The Media Would Never Ask Any Embarrassing Questions. Doctrine Of Drug Czar

Infallibility? Blame Canada, Again.
